title: The Fall of the Water

pages.text:
*The Surveyor's Catechism, Eighteenth Saying: Water is the only honest surveyor. It always finds the level.*

The water in the stream was cold enough to make Isla’s teeth ache, and it moved with a lazy, persistent patience that made her respect it. Joss waded ahead, his black work boots disappearing into the current, while Isla held the wooden staff upright on the riverbed, her boots squelching with every step. They were measuring the drop, or the fall, of the water over the two miles leading up to the old mill.

"Ninety-one feet," Isla said, checking the numbers against her field-book. The ink was smudged where her thumb had brushed it, but the digits were clear. "From here to the wheel."

Joss grinned, water dripping from his sandy hair. "That’s a lot of water, Corrin. Enough to turn a wheel until the sun goes out, if you ask a bridge-wright."

"Ask a mathematician," Isla corrected, scribbling the figure. "Or a surveyor who has to draw a line that doesn’t erode itself into the valley floor within a month." She tapped the page. "A single long arc for the old race. That’s how Hester did it. But we need a steady head. If the slope is too steep, the water chews through the banks. If it’s too flat, it stagnates."

She did the sum in her head, the way Mags did, but slower, more deliberately. Two miles. Ninety-one feet. The river fell about one foot in every hundred and sixteen, a torrent’s slope, far too steep for a channel that meant to keep its banks.

"One in fifteen hundred," she said, the number landing in her mind with a satisfying click. "That’s the gradient for a race that stays put, so we make the water walk the long way round and keep the fall for the wheel. Gentle enough that the water glides rather than fights. It’s the difference between a river and a road."

Joss looked at her, his freckles pale against his flushed cheeks. He didn’t argue. He didn’t need to. He had been listening, counting the stones under his feet, thinking about how the force of that much water would push against the timber. He liked numbers that meant things. He liked that Isla’s numbers meant the ground would hold.

"It’s a good number," he said softly. "Steady. I can build for steady."

Isla smiled, though her fingers were still numb from the cold water. "Then we better get back before the sun sets. We have a valley to keep."
pages.image: Isla in mustard coat and Joss in rust-red shirt wading in a shallow stream, Isla holding a wooden surveying staff upright, Joss looking at her with a respectful smile, cold water splashing around their boots, late afternoon light.

pages.text:
The old mill-race lay in a shadow of silt and moss, a long, dry channel that had once carried the lifeblood of Ennis Vale. The miller walked beside them with the weary pride of a man showing off a broken heirloom. He pointed to the stones lining the channel, cracked and weeping with age.

"The wheel is gone," the miller said, his voice dry. "But the dream is here. The water wants to turn. It just doesn’t know how anymore."

Joss crouched by the remains of the sluice gate, running his hand over the rusted iron hinges. He pulled a piece of charcoal from his apron pocket and began to sketch in the dirt, not on paper, but on the flat stone of the race bed. He drew the wheel, then the shaft, then the gears that would drive the grinding stones.

"Overshot," Joss murmured, his eyes bright with the architecture of force. "The water hits the top of the wheel. Gravity does the work. We don’t need to fight the current; we just need to let it fall."

Isla watched him draw, then looked up the valley. The stream was high today, swollen with the morning rain. She saw where the water spilled over the banks, where it threatened the orchard rows, where it could easily sweep into the village lanes if the sky opened up again.

"We need a spillway," Isla said, her voice cutting through the quiet. "Not just for the wheel. For the village."

The miller looked at her sharply. "A spillway?"

"Yes. A small channel, cut into the high ground on the north side. When the river rises, the water goes over the weir and around the orchard, not through the houses." Isla pointed to the sketch Joss was making. "You build the wheel for the flow you want. I build the spillway for the flow you don’t. They are different jobs, but they are the same land."

Joss looked up from his drawing. He was still smiling, but there was a new sharpness to it. He picked up a stick and tapped the ground where Isla had indicated.

"Then we draw the line for the spillway first," he said. "Because if the village floods, there is no mill. And if there is no mill, there is no reason for any of us to be here."
pages.image: Joss sketching a water wheel design on a flat stone in a dry, mossy channel with charcoal, Isla pointing up the valley, Wynne the miller watching with interest, dappled shade and green moss.

pages.text:
The mill-house was cold, smelling of damp wood and old flour. A single candle burned on the table, its flame trembling in the draft that slipped under the door. Isla and Joss sat on either side of the field-book, their shoulders almost touching, the warmth of their bodies a small, defiant thing against the chill of the room.

The candle had burned down to a stub, a yellow finger of wax. Isla had been calculating the capacity of the race for three hours. The numbers were stubborn, refusing to align. She frowned, her nose brushing the paper, and a smudge of graphite transferred to her skin.

"I’m missing something," she muttered, her voice rough with fatigue. "The volume isn’t matching the fall. If the cross-section is this wide, the velocity must be higher, but that means more erosion. Unless..."

Joss leaned in, his face close to hers. He could smell the ink on her fingers, the faint scent of the candle wax, the clean, sharp smell of her skin. He didn’t look away.

"Unless the channel isn’t rectangular," he said softly. "It’s a trapezoid. The side slopes change the area."

Isla looked up. Her eyes were tired, but bright. She saw the shape he was describing, the way the water would widen as it fell, the way the force would distribute itself. It was a simple thing, a basic principle, but she had been so focused on the height that she had ignored the width.

"You’re right," she whispered. "You’re absolutely right."

Joss reached out, his thumb brushing the graphite smudge from her nose. He didn’t pull away immediately. He stood there, his hand hovering near her cheek, his eyes dark and steady. The candle flickered, casting long shadows across the table. For a moment, the noise of the wind outside ceased to exist. There was only the sound of his breathing, and the stillness of the room, holding its breath like a plumb bob waiting for the line to go true.

"Keep going," he said, his voice rough. "I’m not going anywhere."
pages.image: Close up of Isla and Joss at a wooden table in a dim, cold room, a candle stub burning between them, Joss gently wiping a graphite smudge from Isla's nose, their faces close, warm light on their skin.

pages.text:
Morning came with a gray light that did nothing to hide the arguments. The crew was gathered in the mill yard, the mist still clinging to the ground. Isla stood with the theodolite, the staff planted in the mud. The question on the table was simple, and yet it felt like a weight on her chest: which side of the valley would the new race run on?

"The east side is shorter," Sera said, her voice crisp, cutting through the damp air. She stood apart, her plum coat immaculate, her arms crossed. "Half a mile less. Less timber, less labor. It makes sense."

"It’s also right under the orchard," Joss said, shaking his head. He was leaning against a wagon wheel, his arms crossed, his face set in a line of stubbornness. "When the rain comes, the water will pool. The roots will rot. You’ll have a river where you want to be trees."

Isla looked at the map, then at the valley. The east was efficient. It was the logical choice. It was the choice the Guild would make, the choice that won prizes. But she looked at the orchard, at the rows of apple trees that had survived forty-four years of drift, and she thought of the hands that had planted them.

"The west side," Isla said.

Sera raised an eyebrow. "It’s longer. It’s harder. It’s less efficient."

"It’s longer by half a mile," Isla agreed. "And it keeps the orchard dry. And it keeps the village safe from the runoff. Some people live under that orchard, Sera. They are not a variable in an equation. They are the point."

Joss looked at her, and a slow, wide smile spread across his face. He didn’t look surprised. He looked like a man who had been waiting for the answer, who had known the question was a test, and had passed it.

"I was hoping you would say that," he said, his voice low, meant only for her ears. "I was hoping you cared about the trees more than the time."
pages.image: Isla standing with a theodolite in a misty yard, Sera in a plum coat with arms crossed looking skeptical, Joss leaning against a wagon wheel smiling at Isla, gray morning light.

pages.text:
They began staking the line at noon. The work was slow, a marching of pegs and string that moved down the valley in strict formation. Mags led the way, her red canvas shoes splashing in the mud, the iron cooking pot tied to her back, humming a tune that had no name and no melody. Behind her, Perrin’s two grandchildren, small and serious, carried the stakes, their faces grim with the importance of the task.

Isla walked in the middle, checking the tension of the string, the level of the pegs. She felt the rhythm of it, the steady beat of their steps. It was not fast work. Nor was it glamorous. But it was honest. Every peg was placed with care, every measurement checked twice. The line was a promise, a thread of truth laid across the earth.

Perrin stood on the bank, his white whiskers bristling in the wind. He watched them go, his eyes following the string, the stakes, the people. He did not speak. His hands rested on his stick.

When they reached the bottom of the valley, and the last peg was driven and the string taut, Isla stopped. She looked back up the slope. The line of white flags, the pegs, the people. It looked like a procession. It looked like a road. It looked like a future.

She felt a tiredness deep in her bones, a weariness that was not unpleasant, but heavy. It was the burden of responsibility, the gravity of truth. She looked at Joss, who was wiping his hands on his apron, and at Mags, who was already pulling out her pot to start the fire.

Isla took a breath. The air was cold, but it was clean. She had never been so happy, or so tired, in her life. And for the first time, she felt like she belonged there, in the dirt, with the string and the stakes.
